NF5 Family Limited Partnership, Intervenor, Opposing Link M22
SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26–16349
PUC DOCKET NO. 59475

INITIAL POST HEARING BRIEF OF INTERVENOR NF5 FAMILY LIMITED PARTNERSHIP
COMES NOW, NF5 Family Limited Partnership, by Wade Noelke, to submit its initial brief pursuant to SOAH Order No. 6 in this cause.
Introduction
1. 	The NF5 Family Limited Partnership (“NF5”) is negatively impacted and opposes Link M22, specifically on Tracts 508 and 509. NF5 opposes Routes 547, 548, 295, 296 and 297, which are on Link M22.
2.	Wade Noelke filed a Direct Testimony (3997) on behalf of NF5, explaining its opposition in detail.
3.	NF5 participated in the Hearing on the Merits through Wade Noelke. NF5 and Wade Noelke did not call any witnesses, and no party called NF5 or Wade Noelke as a witness. This Court admitted “Exhibit 1 Wade Noelke Direct Testimony on Behalf of NF5 Family Limited Partnership” (“Wade Noelke Direct Testimony”) as evidence.


4.	Applicants at the Hearing on the Merits failed to admit any evidence directly rebutting
Wade Noelke’s claims as described in his Direct Testimony. On appeal of this matter, a contested case under the Texas Administrative Procedure Act, Applicants will lack the necessary substantial evidence required for them to locate their proposed 765 kV line on NF5’s family ranch. See PURA § 15.001 and Tex Gov’t Code § 2001.174.
      5.    Further, it would be unreasonable for the Commission to place the transmission line on NF5’s family ranch for the statutory factors below which the PUC must consider, and which the Applicants did not consider when designing the alternative routes using Link M22 on Tracts 508 and 509.

    II.	PURA Factors
Community Values – PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)
Under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A), the Commission must consider community values. The 
Commission has interpreted "community values" as "a shared appreciation of an area or other natural or human resource by a national, regional, or local community." PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A); PUC Docket No. 43878 Application of Brazos Electric Power Cooperative, Inc. to Amend a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for A 138 - kV Double Circuit Transmission Line in Collin and Denton Counties, Final Order, para. 46.
	Noelke testified about the community values present on NF5’s family ranch, noting the continued raising of cattle and other agriculture on the ranch “since 1880.” Exhibit 1: Wade Noelke Direct Testimony on Behalf of NF5 Family Limited Partnership, at p. 8. He further testified about the “high-quality wildlife” and “hunting opportunities” on the ranch, the Noelke family’s “preserving and improving the land’s natural condition for future generations” which has continued since 1880, and the many “recreational opportunities” including “shooting sports” and “[lodging and] camping” which continue to occur on the NF5 family ranch since 1880.
	Noelke’s testimony showed how the NF5 family ranch contributes significantly to the community values of the Menard and surrounding Hill Country area, specifically in the areas of history, family ranching legacy, current ranching, hunting, and recreational uses. Further, as mentioned above, the Texas Department of Agriculture officially recognized the Noelke-Wilhelm’s ranch, of which NF5 is a part, for its contributions to “Texas’ historic and traditional ranching operations which helped develop the state and continues to play an important economic role today.” Id. at pp. 5, 8.
	Noelke further explained on how the 765 KV line would impact the community values. He noted it would bring “dangerous electricity flow and electromagnetic fields to our ranch’s occupants and wildlife,” “devastate the terrain it is placed on and likely push out any wildlife and humans who use that area,” “be nearly impossible to conserve an artificially-cleared out area that is alien to the currently native condition of the lands,” and likely push out “guests and family members...[who could not] driv[e] next to, shoot near, and hik[e] near due to the electromagnetic fields, sparks, and potential fire hazard during storms.” Id. at pp. 10–11.
	Therefore, locating the 765 KV transmission line on NF5’s family ranch would harm its ability to uphold community values. It would also be unreasonable to place the line on NF5’s property for the same reasons.

	Aesthetic and Historical Values – PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C)
To measure the aesthetic value under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C), the PUC stated, "[A]esthetic impacts to visual resources exist when the right-of-way, lines and/or structures of a transmission line system create an intrusion into, or substantially alter, the character of the existing view.” PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C); Docket No. 45866, Application of LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to Amend a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for the Round Rock - Leander 138-KV Transmission Line in Williamson County, Final Order, para. 60. In determining this impact, the PUC advises, "The significance of the impact is directly related to the quality of the view in natural scenic areas, [and] the importance of the existing setting in the use and enjoyment of an area.” Docket No. 45866, Application of LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to Amend a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for the Round Rock - Leander 138-KV Transmission Line in Williamson County, Final Order, para. 60.
Wade Noelke’s Direct Testimony gave an in-depth analysis of how a 765-KV transmission line, with an approximately 200-foot width and 175-height on average, would significantly and permanently damage the current, native aesthetic value of the NF5 family ranch.
Noelke testified that presently, “Live oaks and mesquites [are] the tallest objects on the land, thereby maintain[ing] the native environmental landscape from centuries ago.” Exhibit 1: Wade Noelke Direct Testimony on Behalf of NF5 Family Limited Partnership, at p. 9. Noelke further added “the vast majority of the ranch [is] clear [aesthetically] and in [its] native vegetative conditions, with “only a small 10-ft telephone line” that impacts the aesthetic of the NF5 ranch near the houses. Id. at pp. 9–10.
However, Noelke showed the significant and permanent damage that the 765 KV lines would create when he stated, “The transmission line would cause massive harm to the natural environment, especially in the direct middle of our ranch, adding massive metal structures to an otherwise nearly pristine natural Texas Hill Country landscape.” Id. at p. 10. Noelke added the line “would likely clear out much of the brush permanently, and the trees would take decades to regrow if at all...and the rolling hills would suffer with massive excavations and maintenance likely destroying the environmental flow of the land.” Id.
Thus, the NF5’s current live oak, mesquite tree, and rolling hills’ aesthetic would be substantially intruded upon and substantially altered by the addition of tall, metal lines of man-made creation into the middle of a native, Texas hill-country setting preserved since the Noelke-Wilhelms acquired the ranch over a century ago. The native aesthetic would be wiped out, with the metal structure being the tallest structure on the ranch. Further, it would cut in the direct middle of the ranch, where until now no man-made device could be seen in the ranch. 
Additionally, the 200-foot width would tear up the rolling hills, creating trenches and tearing up the native flow of the current land, as Noelke pointed out. Id. at 10. The hills in the middle of the ranch would likely be gone. Id.
As a result of the 765-KV transmission lines’ likely significant and permanent damage to the current, native aesthetic of the NF5 family ranch, it would be unreasonable to place such lines on the NF5’s family ranch.

Historical Values:
Under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C), the Commission must consider the historical values and the impact of certain transmission line routes on the community. PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C).
	Noelke testified to the important historical values of the NF5 family ranch. Noelke stated “My family has owned and developed this land since 1880 [when]...Joanna Wilhelm...created the ranch,” formerly using and continuing to use the NF5 family ranch “for historic Texas purposes” including “cattle grazing and sheep grazing...hunting, conservation, and recreational values that increase [his] family’s [and the guests’] connection with the historic use and enjoyment of the land.” Exhibit 1: Wade Noelke Direct Testimony on Behalf of NF5 Family Limited Partnership, at p. 10. And as referenced above, The Texas Department of Agriculture actually recognized the Noelke-Wilhelm ranch—of which the NF5 family ranch is a part—for its contributions to “Texas’ historic and traditional ranching operations which helped develop the state and continues to play an important economic role today.” Id. at p. 8. 
	Thus, the NF5 family ranch clearly has and continues to exhibit major Texas historical values, including livestock grazing, hunting, conservation, and recreation, which have and continue to make Texas a leader in honoring its heritage and offering its citizens a real economic path for success moving forward.
	The 765 KV lines would likely destroy most or all of the historic values, including by “devastat[ing] the terrain [the line] is placed on and likely push out any wildlife and humans who use that area,” harming the historic ranching-grazing uses by “los[ing] at least 200 feet of grass in width, and likely over a half-mile in length,” making it hard to “conserve an artificially-cleared out area that is alien to the currently native condition of the lands,” and likely pushing out “guests and family members...[who could not] driv[e] next to, shoot near, and hik[e] near due to the electromagnetic fields, sparks, and potential fire hazard during storms.”  Id. at pp. 10–11.
Thus, it would be unreasonable to place the 765 KV line on the NF5’s family ranch. 

	Environmental Integrity – PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D)

Under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D), the Commission must factor in preserving environmental 
integrity when deciding which route to select. PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D).
	As Noelke testified and as referenced above, “A 765 KV, 200 feet wide and 175 feet tall line would significantly impair the environmental integrity of the land, where currently our live oaks and mesquite are the tallest parts of the land...Because there is no major structure cutting through the land and thus keeping in the ranchlands’ natural and native conditions, the transmission line would cause massive harm to the natural environment...especially in the direct middle of our ranch, adding massive metal structures to an otherwise nearly pristine natural Texas Hill Country landscape.” Exhibit 1: Wade Noelke Direct Testimony on Behalf of NF5 Family Limited Partnership, at pp. 9–10. Noelke specified that if the line is placed on the M22 transmission route, the metal structure would “DIRECTLY CUT OUR NOELKE-WILHELM RANCH IN HALF, LIKELY DESTROYING THE MAJORITY OF OUR RANCH.” Id. at 12. 
Noelke was being honest in his assessment of the environmental damage the 765 KV line would cause to the NF5 family ranch. The 765 KV line would indeed cut through the very middle of the NF5’s ranch, cause “massive excavations” flattening the “rolling hills,” deter wildlife and humans who use the area due to the line’s intrusive presence and “loud” humming of the lines, and “clear out much of the brush” and “live oaks” which have stood there for over a hundred years in the native condition of the land. Id. at pp. 6, 10, 11. The native vegetation of the ranch would likely suffer permanent injury due to the major environmental disruption from the line’s installation and post-existence, severely harming the environmental integrity of the ranch.
	Oncor and the LCRA (“Applicants”) did not appear to take the statutory factor of environmental integrity seriously on the NF5 family ranch. Because the environmental integrity would be devastated by the transmission line for the reasons above, it would be unreasonable to place the line on the NF5’s family ranch.

Paralleling – 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(i)-(iii) criteria

The Commission must consider "(i) whether the routes parallel or utilize existing
compatible rights-of-way for electric facilities, including the use of vacant positions on existing
multiple circuit transmission lines; (ii) whether the routes parallel or utilize other existing
compatible rights-of-way, including roads, highways, railroads, or telephone utility rights-of
way; (iii) whether the routes parallel property lines or other natural or cultural features; and (iv)
whether the routes conform with the policy of prudent avoidance. 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).
Thus, the extent to which a route follows existing corridors is a key factor in selecting the
route of a utility line.
	In Noelke’s testimony, he honestly and passionately noted how the proposed route on the M22 link would “DIRECTLY CUT OUR NOELKE-WILHELM RANCH IN HALF, LIKELY DESTROYING THE MAJORITY OF OUR RANCH.” Exhibit 1: Wade Noelke Direct Testimony on Behalf of NF5 Family Limited Partnership, at p. 12. As stated above, a 175-tall metal structure cutting through the middle of the NF5’s property would likely devastate the use of NF5’s family ranch by “limiting available use of the grazing lands, hunting because wildlife will likely avoid the metal contraption and noise, conservation because it would be nearly impossible to conserve an artificially-cleared out area that is alien to the currently native condition of the lands, and recreationally because guests and family members would likely not want to spend time near the structures, and could be dangerous when being next to.” Id. at pp. 11–12.
Because the Applicants’ proposed route on Link M22 does not parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way for electric facilities, does not parallel or utilize other existing
compatible rights-of way, including roads, highways, or telephone utility rights-of
way, or even parallel any property lines or other natural or cultural features, it would be unreasonable to place the line straight down the middle of NF5’s entire property. The effect of such action would, as Noelke has repeatedly stated, “DESTROY THE MAJORITY OF OUR RANCH.” Id. at p. 12.
	In the event the M22 link is chosen for Applicant’s line, Noelke asks the Commission or even the Applicants to respect the NF5 family ranch by moving the lines to the edge of the ranch, as not to destroy the NF5’s ranch as a whole.

    III.   Additional Arguments

As mentioned earlier, NF5 asserts Applicants completely failed to weigh or consider the Texas Department of Agriculture’s (“TDA”) 2024 Family Land Heritage Program recognition of the Noelke-Wilhelm ranch, which the Noelkes and Wilhelms have proudly owned and responsibly managed since 1880.  Id. at p. 5.

i. Such failure means Applicants improperly weighed the required statutory factors related to NF5’s family ranch. It is unreasonable and unjust for an important state agency, the TDA, to recognize the historical, community, and aesthetic values of the Noelke-Wilhelm’s ranch, which includes the current NF5 ranch, while a different state agency, the PUC, ignores such significant values a mere 2 years later.
ii. Applicants blame TDA’s failure to adopt reliable data sets on the location of these recognized properties as the reason they did not consider this recognition.  See RFI 1-06 in Gretchen Noelke Exh. 2.
iii. Notwithstanding the lack of data sets, Applicants conceded in cross during the Hearing on the Merits that it could consider ranches with this recognition as historical.  See Transcript for June 9, 2026 at pp. 73-76.  The Texas Department of Transportation, a state agency, considers these historical ranches.  Id.
iv. Thus, it would be unreasonable to place the 765 KV transmission line on NF5’s ranch.
 NF5 asserts that, as applied, amended PURA  §37.057 is not a grant of authority to the Applicants to disregard landowner Due Course of Law rights under the Texas Constitution, Tex. Const. art. I, § 19, Due Process rights under the U.S. Constitution, U.S. Const. Amend XIV, § 1 or those rights found in the Texas Administrative Procedure Act at Texas Gov’t Code § 2001.051. The expedited 180-day calendar for these proceedings necessarily meant that it could not respond to or present evidence and argument on every issue in the case, as it is entitled pursuant to Texas Gov’t Code § 2001.051. It is not arguing for a declaration that PURA  §37.057 is unconstitutional, only that how it was applied in this proceeding (that has as many as 700+ intervenors) is unconstitutional and in deprivation of her rights under Texas Gov’t Code § 2001.051.
Finally, NF5 supports the positions taken by the American Stewards of Liberty (ALS) on the deferral of the determination of need issues, as well as the Amici Curiae brief filed by certain Texas Legislators in this case. See Item 6139 for the Amici brief and a summary of the positions taken by ALS.  Great weight should be given to the testimony of PUC staff member Mr. Poole by Intervenor Ms. Graci.  She asked him whether the load demand Applicants’ project should be re-evaluated since Google and others were developing gas-fired power generation projects for data centers. Mr. Poole stated, “As the situation on the ground changes, then perhaps a re-evaluation is warranted.”  Transcript for Tuesday June 9, 2026 at p. 289-290.
  

IV.    Conclusion 
NF5 respectfully requests this Honorable Court consider its arguments above. Further, NF5 respectfully requests this Honorable Court to find Applicants’ alternative Routes of 547, 548, 295, 296, and 297 using the M22 Link, specifically on tracts 508 and 509, to be unreasonable for the proposed transmission line.
Signed June 19, 2026
Respectfully submitted,

/s/ Wade Noelke
Wade Noelke
NF5 Family Limited Partnership
Intervenor

CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE
I certify that a true and correct copy of the foregoing document was served on all parties and counsel of record on June 19, 2026 with PUC Procedural Rule 22.74 and Orders issued in Docket No. 59182 and 59475.

/s/ Wade Noelke
Wade Noelke
NF5 Family Limited Partnership
Intervenor
